Before the vote closes

Five concrete steps would make the result easier to trust, whichever way the vote goes.

  1. Publish an interest register

    Directors, Think Tank members, ERIS signers, validators, large voting accounts and contractors should disclose relevant grant, payment, delegation, hosting and voting-contract interests at entity or handle level.

    See the relationships

  2. Declare contract voting intentions

    Publish the intended ampLUNA-hub and vAMP prop-gauge actions before those contracts vote. At capture, the gauge had zero votes and the hub had no native 4853 ballot.

    How contract voting works

  3. Complete internal votes before validator ballots

    A validator following a DAO mandate should wait for that DAO’s final result. Lion DAO changed its native ballot while its own A33 vote remained open; both positions ultimately became YES.

    Review the sequence

  4. Preserve independent ballots

    Validators and holders should vote on the proposal’s merits. A hub vote changes its native delegator power; it does not prove that validators share ownership or instructions.

    Read the counterevidence

  5. Preserve the record for independent review

    Retain ballots, admin/configuration state, DAO messages, payment schedules and responses. Proposal 4853 itself calls for an impartial investigation; it does not predetermine liability.

    Open the evidence library

What the evidence supports

Credible governance questions, with limits stated beside each finding.

Outcome-changing voting capability is concentrated

A hypothetical full ampLUNA-hub YES would move the captured 4853 tally from failing to passing. One unattributed account can meet the vAMP participation quorum by itself.

Not established: that either action has occurred, or that the large account is controlled by ERIS.

Test the scenario

Oversight participation and disclosure need review

The Think Tank’s four substantive veto proposals received no YES or NO ballots. Members also have grant, payment or commercial relationships relevant to independence.

Not established: deliberate inactivity, vote buying or common ownership.

Review all six members

The contract handover is incomplete

ERIS proposal 9 transferred two CosmWasm upgrade admins to the Phoenix board. It did not change the hub’s stored owner or ICS20’s internal governance contract; wider Treasury/TLA roles also remain.

Not established: exclusive key custody or the absence of any off-chain authorization.

Compare admin and owner

Related-party payments need consistent controls

Board beneficiaries participated in some payment decisions. Recurring contributor payments, related-party OTC trades and monthly validator-to-ERIS transfers require agreements, pricing and acceptance records.

Not established: that gross funding is personal profit, or that every large transfer is compensation.

Review payment categories

A single-bloc theory does not fit the record.

Smart Stake and Ceres voted NO WITH VETO; HighStakes voted ABSTAIN. Eleven reviewed allocation-linked validators had no current ballot. Directors have dissented on material proposals, and A272 failed.

These facts do not erase concentration or conflict concerns. They do require analysis that includes all stakeholders and alternatives.

Review the whole stakeholder map

After 4853: make independence structural

Short-term fairness needs longer-term controls.

  • Related-party disclosure, recusal and independent approval
  • A functioning Think Tank with notifications, complete messages and published rationales
  • Separate upgrade, configuration, treasury and voting powers with a verified handover
  • Transparent delegations, contract voting and validator mandates
  • Deliverable-based payments, OTC pricing review and independent reconciliation
